questions.question: What does it mean for $f$ to attain a global maximum at $x_{\mathrm{max}}$ on $X$?
questions.explanation: A global maximum at $x_{\mathrm{max}}$ means $f(x_{\mathrm{max}})\ge f(x)$ for every $x\in X$; the output dominates all outputs on the entire domain.
questions.source_support: The definition states $f(x_{\mathrm{max}})\geq f(x)$ for all $x\in X$.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: Comparison with a single point is insufficient; a global maximum must dominate $f(x)$ for every $x\in X$, not just one.
The inequality $f(x_{\mathrm{max}})\le f(x)$ for all $x$ defines a global minimum, not a maximum.
The extremal value need not be zero; $f(x)=-x^2+5$ attains its global maximum $5$ at $x=0$, with $f(0)=5\neq 0$.

questions.question: On what kind of domain can a continuous function fail to attain a global maximum?

A global extremum can only occur if the domain is $\mathbb{R}$.
A global extremum must be both a maximum and a minimum.
questions.explanation: A global extremum may fail to exist on an unbounded domain (where $f$ can escape to infinity) or an open domain (where the limiting endpoint value is not attained).

questions.source_support: Global extrema need not exist without a closed, bounded domain.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: Functions need not have extrema; $f(x)=x$ on $\mathbb R$ has neither a global maximum nor a global minimum.
The domain need not be all reals; in fact $\mathbb R$ is exactly where $f(x)=x$ fails to have a global extremum, while $[0,1]$ (not all reals) guarantees one for continuous $f$.
A function may have only one type of extremum; $f(x)=x^2$ on $\mathbb R$ has a global minimum but no global maximum.
